Introduction Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, has been a significant public health burden in the tropical and subtropical areas since the early 20th century [15]. The causative agent for this disease is dengue virus, a single positive-stranded RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae, with strains characterized by five serotypes [36]. Dengue virus is primarily transmitted by female mosquitoes of the Aedes genus that includes species such as Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus [31]. At present, it is estimated that around 400 million people are infected with dengue annually, and about half a million require hospital care [3,22,36]. Common symptoms of dengue include sudden-onset fever, headache, vomiting, and a characteristic skin rash. Severe cases of dengue infection can cause health complications such as dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, which may lead to death if not treated in a timely manner [12]. Individuals infected with dengue virus will go through an exposed (or, latent) period of 3–8 days without exhibiting any symptoms [16]. These asymptomatic individuals can infect local mosquitoes which go on to bite other people and spread the infection to larger human populations. They also pose a threat to transfusion recipients through infected blood products [18]. Furthermore, asymptomatic individuals can be re-infected, referred to as a secondary infection, through mosquitoes carrying a different strain of dengue virus and become symptomatic with more severe health conditions [24]. The mechanism for the different viral serotypes to cause severe dengue disease is not entirely clear at present, but it is mostly linked to the Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE), a phenomenon where pre-existing antibodies do not neutralize but rather enhance the new infection [2]. Hence, asymptomatic infectious individuals play a significant role in shaping the overall pattern of dengue transmission and spread. Quantifying such a role is essential in understanding the transmission dynamics of dengue and in designing effective prevention and intervention strategies. Like many other infectious disease, the transmission of dengue exhibits strong heterogeneity among different human hosts. One of the most important factors to reflect such heterogeneity is the chronological age. Individuals of different ages may have different social behaviors, mobility levels, and contact dynamics, which subsequently lead to different infection risk, disease severity, survival capacity, and recovery ability. In particular, children are more vulnerable than adults because of their immature immune systems, and they have higher risk of severe complications for dengue [28,33]. Identifying such transmission characteristics associated with different age groups and classifying such an age structure in a dengue model are critical toward a holistic understanding of dengue transmission dynamics. Numerous mathematical models have been published for the transmission dynamics of dengue [1,11– 13,16,18–20,22,24,26,29,31]. For example, Esteva and Vargas studied the coexistence of different serotypes of dengue virus [11]. Pongsumpun and Samana published a model for the primary infection dynamics of dengue that involves both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals [26]. Jan and Xiao modeled the effect of partial immunity from the susceptible human population on the transmission of dengue and performed an optimal control study for disease prevention and intervention [19]. Rashkov and Kooi integrated the vector dynamics of mosquitoes into the human transmission of dengue [29]. Rocha et al. considered the role of seasonality in dengue infection dynamics [30]. Ferguson et al. proposed a multi-strain model to investigate the effect of ADE on dengue transmission [13]. Aguiar et al. studied the differences between the primary and secondary infections of dengue in the presence of seasonality and multiple viral strains [1]. Kabir and Tanimoto conducted a cost-efficiency analysis for the effect of ADE on dengue vaccination [20]. In addition, a number of other mathematical models for dengue are surveyed in a recent review article [2]. There is no doubt that these modeling studies have substantially advanced our knowledge in the transmission dynamics of dengue and in the design of effective control strategies for this disease. However, the fundamental role of the asymptomatic infection in dengue transmission within a heterogeneous host population is only partially addressed at present. Particularly, our understanding of the intertwined relationship among the primary and secondary infections, the asymptomatic and symptomatic states, and the different age groups, remains limited. In the present paper, we propose a new mathematical model for the transmission dynamics of dengue based on the age-structured modeling technique. Age-structured models have been employed in many epidemiological studies and have provided useful guidelines for disease control [5,8–10,12,21,22,25,27,32,35,37, 38]. A few of these have been specifically devoted to dengue [12,22,27]. Our proposed study differs from the prior age-structured models in the integration of several factors that are important toward a deeper understanding of dengue dynamics. Our modeling framework will incorporate both mosquito-to-human and human-to-mosquito transmission routes, will include both symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious hosts, will place a special emphasis on the secondary infection from asymptomatic individuals, and will connect all these components in an age-structured setting. The model consists of a strongly nonlinear system of coupled differential and integral equations, which will be rigorously analyzed throughout this study. X. Li et al. / J. Math. Anal. We have placed a special emphasis on the asymptomatic individuals and their interaction with mosquitoes and other human hosts. Our results highlight the roles of the asymptomatic hosts and secondary infection in shaping dengue transmission under a heterogeneous setting that couples the host and vector populations and that involves different age groups. A detailed mathematical analysis has been conducted for this model using the basic reproduction number R derived in Section3. It is proved that the disease-free steady state is locally asymptotically stable if R < 0 0 1 and globally asymptotically stable if R <1 −ς for some ς >0. It is also shown that when R >1, there 0 0 exists at least one endemic steady state and the disease is both weakly and strongly uniformly persistent. Numerical simulation results confirm these analytical predictions. Additionally, sufficient conditions are established for the existence of multiple endemic steady states when R <1which could lead to a backward bifurcation. The threshold dynamics results indicate that to eradicate the disease, it may not be sufficient to simply reduce the basic reproduction number R below unity. Instead, control measures should be made to further reduce R so that it is outside the interval for the possible backward bifurcation and falls within the region of global asymptotic stability for the disease-free steady state. The expression for R includes contributions from both the human and vector populations, underscoring the importance of controlling both the infected hosts and mosquitoes in the management of dengue. Meanwhile, the equation of R represents the two transmission routes associated with the symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious hosts. Therefore, dengue control strategies should target both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals to effectively reduce the value of R . In particular, reducing the reinfection intensity factor σwould directly decrease the contribution of the asymptomatic individuals to R . If new diagnostic testing methods, such as those for COVID-19, can be developed and widely implemented to rapidly identify people infected with dengue, especially those asymptomatic individuals, that would substantially reduce the transmission risk of dengue. Moreover, our model and results also build a foundation for a study of optimal control strategies for dengue based on different age groups. The transmission dynamics of dengue are complex, and there are many factors that are potentially important and that have not been considered in the present work. These include, but are not limited to, delay from actual infection to host awareness of the infection, effect of ADE on the transmission rates, heterogeneity in the spatial spread of the disease, and impact of dengue vaccination. 1. Introduction
Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, has been a significant public health burden in the tropical and
subtropical areas since the early 20th century [15]. The causative agent for this disease is dengue virus, a
single positive-stranded RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae, with strains characterized by five serotypes
[36]. Dengue virus is primarily transmitted by female mosquitoes of the Aedes genus that includes species
such as Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus [31]. At present, it is estimated that around 400 million people
are infected with dengue annually, and about half a million require hospital care [3,22,36].
Common symptoms of dengue include sudden-onset fever, headache, vomiting, and a characteristic skin
rash. Severe cases of dengue infection can cause health complications such as dengue haemorrhagic fever
and dengue shock syndrome, which may lead to death if not treated in a timely manner [12]. Individuals
infected with dengue virus will go through an exposed (or, latent) period of 3–8 days without exhibiting
any symptoms [16]. They become infectious after the latent period, but the majority (over 80%) of the

cases with a primary infection remain asymptomatic [36]. These asymptomatic individuals can infect local
mosquitoes which go on to bite other people and spread the infection to larger human populations. They also
pose a threat to transfusion recipients through infected blood products [18]. Furthermore, asymptomatic
individuals can be re-infected, referred to as a secondary infection, through mosquitoes carrying a different
strain of dengue virus and become symptomatic with more severe health conditions [24]. The mechanism for
the different viral serotypes to cause severe dengue disease is not entirely clear at present, but it is mostly
linked to the Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE), a phenomenon where pre-existing antibodies do
not neutralize but rather enhance the new infection [2]. Hence, asymptomatic infectious individuals play a
significant role in shaping the overall pattern of dengue transmission and spread. Quantifying such a role is
essential in understanding the transmission dynamics of dengue and in designing effective prevention and
intervention strategies.
Like many other infectious disease, the transmission of dengue exhibits strong heterogeneity among
different human hosts. One of the most important factors to reflect such heterogeneity is the chronological
age. Individuals of different ages may have different social behaviors, mobility levels, and contact dynamics,
which subsequently lead to different infection risk, disease severity, survival capacity, and recovery ability.
In particular, children are more vulnerable than adults because of their immature immune systems, and
they have higher risk of severe complications for dengue [28,33]. Identifying such transmission characteristics
associated with different age groups and classifying such an age structure in a dengue model are critical
toward a holistic understanding of dengue transmission dynamics.
Numerous mathematical models have been published for the transmission dynamics of dengue [1,11–
13,16,18–20,22,24,26,29,31]. For example, Esteva and Vargas studied the coexistence of different serotypes
of dengue virus [11]. Pongsumpun and Samana published a model for the primary infection dynamics of
dengue that involves both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals [26]. Jan and Xiao modeled the effect
of partial immunity from the susceptible human population on the transmission of dengue and performed an
optimal control study for disease prevention and intervention [19]. Rashkov and Kooi integrated the vector
dynamics of mosquitoes into the human transmission of dengue [29]. Rocha et al. considered the role of
seasonality in dengue infection dynamics [30]. Ferguson et al. proposed a multi-strain model to investigate
the effect of ADE on dengue transmission [13]. Aguiar et al. studied the differences between the primary
and secondary infections of dengue in the presence of seasonality and multiple viral strains [1]. Kabir and
Tanimoto conducted a cost-efficiency analysis for the effect of ADE on dengue vaccination [20]. In addition,
a number of other mathematical models for dengue are surveyed in a recent review article [2]. There is no
doubt that these modeling studies have substantially advanced our knowledge in the transmission dynamics
of dengue and in the design of effective control strategies for this disease. However, the fundamental role of
the asymptomatic infection in dengue transmission within a heterogeneous host population is only partially
addressed at present. Particularly, our understanding of the intertwined relationship among the primary
and secondary infections, the asymptomatic and symptomatic states, and the different age groups, remains
limited.
In the present paper, we propose a new mathematical model for the transmission dynamics of dengue
based on the age-structured modeling technique. Age-structured models have been employed in many epi-
demiological studies and have provided useful guidelines for disease control [5,8–10,12,21,22,25,27,32,35,37,
38]. A few of these have been specifically devoted to dengue [12,22,27]. Our proposed study differs from
the prior age-structured models in the integration of several factors that are important toward a deeper
understanding of dengue dynamics. Our modeling framework will incorporate both mosquito-to-human and
human-to-mosquito transmission routes, will include both symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious hosts,
will place a special emphasis on the secondary infection from asymptomatic individuals, and will connect
all these components in an age-structured setting. The model consists of a strongly nonlinear system of
coupled differential and integral equations, which will be rigorously analyzed throughout this study.

7. Conclusions
We have presented a novel age-structured model to investigate the transmission dynamics of dengue. Our
model links the interaction between the human hosts of different ages and mosquitoes, includes both the
symptomatic and asymptomatic classes, and incorporates the effects of primary and secondary infections.
We have placed a special emphasis on the asymptomatic individuals and their interaction with mosquitoes
and other human hosts. Our results highlight the roles of the asymptomatic hosts and secondary infection
in shaping dengue transmission under a heterogeneous setting that couples the host and vector populations
and that involves different age groups.
A detailed mathematical analysis has been conducted for this model using the basic reproduction number
R derived in Section3. It is proved that the disease-free steady state is locally asymptotically stable if R <
0 0
1 and globally asymptotically stable if R <1 −ς for some ς >0. It is also shown that when R >1, there
0 0
exists at least one endemic steady state and the disease is both weakly and strongly uniformly persistent.
Numerical simulation results confirm these analytical predictions. Additionally, sufficient conditions are
established for the existence of multiple endemic steady states when R <1which could lead to a backward
0
bifurcation.
The threshold dynamics results indicate that to eradicate the disease, it may not be sufficient to simply
reduce the basic reproduction number R below unity. Instead, control measures should be made to further
0
reduce R so that it is outside the interval for the possible backward bifurcation and falls within the region
0
of global asymptotic stability for the disease-free steady state. The expression for R includes contributions
0
from both the human and vector populations, underscoring the importance of controlling both the infected
hosts and mosquitoes in the management of dengue. Meanwhile, the equation of R represents the two
0
transmission routes associated with the symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious hosts. Therefore, dengue
control strategies should target both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals to effectively reduce the
value of R . In particular, reducing the reinfection intensity factor σwould directly decrease the contribution
0
of the asymptomatic individuals to R . If new diagnostic testing methods, such as those for COVID-19,
0
can be developed and widely implemented to rapidly identify people infected with dengue, especially those
asymptomatic individuals, that would substantially reduce the transmission risk of dengue. Moreover, our
model and results also build a foundation for a study of optimal control strategies for dengue based on
different age groups.
The transmission dynamics of dengue are complex, and there are many factors that are potentially
important and that have not been considered in the present work. These include, but are not limited to,
delay from actual infection to host awareness of the infection, effect of ADE on the transmission rates,
heterogeneity in the spatial spread of the disease, and impact of dengue vaccination. We plan to study these
topics in our future research.
